analysis.one_liner: Makes registering and voting easier, requires disclosure of big campaign money, and tightens ethics rules for federal officials.
analysis.headline: All 50 Democratic and independent senators voted to open debate on the bill, but the 50-49 vote fell short of the 60 needed, and it never got a real floor vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required states to offer automatic, same-day, online, early, and mail voting in federal elections; limited purging voters from the rolls; restored voting rights to people finishing federal felony sentences; and replaced partisan-drawn congressional districts with independent commissions. It would also have required disclosure of big-money campaign spending, created a small-donor public financing system for candidates, and imposed new ethics rules, including a code of conduct for Supreme Court justices and disclosure of ten years of tax returns by presidents, vice presidents, and their top challengers.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary voters gain most: people who move often, work hours that conflict with polling times, lack documents, live with disabilities, or live on tribal lands would find registering and voting easier under automatic, same-day, online, early, and mail voting requirements [S2][S3]. Citizens released from federal prison regain the vote [S3]. Voters in both parties gain from independent redistricting commissions replacing districts drawn by incumbent lawmakers [S2]. Small donors gain leverage because candidates would be financed partly with public matching funds instead of relying on large checks [S2]. The public gains disclosure of who pays for political ads and spending, tighter lobbying and revolving-door rules, a Supreme Court code of conduct, and tax-return disclosure by presidents, vice presidents, and their challengers [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: All voters, especially those facing registration barriers

how_it_helps.text: Requires every state to register eligible citizens automatically from government records unless they decline, and to offer same-day and online registration, cutting the paperwork that keeps eligible voters off the rolls.

Requires early voting and vote-by-mail in federal elections nationwide, and sets standards for drop boxes, polling place access for people with disabilities and voters on tribal lands, and counting provisional ballots.
Limits when voters can be removed from registration lists and restricts 'voter caging' challenges, and restores federal voting rights to citizens once they complete a felony sentence.
Requires congressional districts to be drawn by independent state commissions instead of the incumbent lawmakers who currently draw them, and bans mid-decade redistricting.
Expands disclosure of campaign spending, including online political ads, tightens the ban on foreign money in elections, and requires campaigns to report contacts with foreign agents.
Creates an alternative public financing system for Senate and presidential candidates built on small-dollar donations, reducing candidates' dependence on large donors.

Imposes a code of conduct on federal judges including Supreme Court justices, restricts the lobbying revolving door, bars House members from serving on for-profit company boards, and requires the president, vice president, and major candidates to disclose ten years of tax returns.
Provides federal grants for paper-ballot voting systems and risk-limiting election audits, and requires intelligence agencies to share election-threat information with state election officials.

analysis.who_pays: Large donors, super PACs, and dark-money nonprofit groups would face disclosure and coordination rules; lobbying firms and foreign agents would face broader registration and a new Justice Department enforcement unit; companies would lose easy access to former procurement officers and other revolving-door hires; and members of Congress would lose perks like serving on for-profit boards and quietly settling workplace claims with Treasury money [S2][S3]. State and local election offices would carry the burden of rebuilding registration, voting, and redistricting systems, though the bill provides federal grants for compliance and equipment [S3]. Taxpayers would fund the new public financing program [S2].
analysis.who_pays_short: Big-money donors, lobbying firms, and state election offices

drawbacks.text: The bill overrides state control of election administration with hundreds of mandates, and state and local election offices would have to rebuild registration, voting, and redistricting systems on federal deadlines even with the grants provided — a heavy administrative lift that good-faith critics in both parties flagged.
The small-donor public financing system would be paid for by taxpayers, a recurring cost that continues every election cycle.

It channels all lawsuits challenging the law's constitutionality into a single federal district court in Washington, D.C., an unusual arrangement that concentrates review of a sweeping law in one venue.

The bill's sheer breadth — voting, campaign finance, and ethics changes touching every branch of government — made it difficult to evaluate as a package, and the Senate Rules Committee held hearings but never voted to report it favorably.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains are broad and concrete: easier registration and voting for millions, public knowledge of who funds campaigns, and districts no longer drawn by the politicians who run in them. The costs are real but ordinary: administrative strain on state election offices (offset by federal grants), a recurring taxpayer bill for public financing, and a defensible federalism objection to Washington dictating how states run elections. A fair process would have forced those trade-offs into open floor debate and amendment; instead the bill died without one, so the public never saw which parts could have survived scrutiny and which should have been dropped.

outcome.mechanism: A vote to clear the way for floor debate needed 60 senators; it got 50 and failed, so the bill never came up for an up-or-down vote before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Merkley introduced the bill on March 17, 2021, and it drew 48 cosponsors — 46 Democrats and 2 independents, essentially the entire Senate Democratic conference.
The bill went to the Senate Rules and Administration Committee, which held hearings, but the committee never voted to report the bill favorably, leaving it stuck.

On August 11, 2021, the Senate voted on a motion to discharge the committee and open debate under an agreement (S. Res. 27) that set a 60-vote threshold; the vote failed 50-49, with all 48 Democrats and 2 independents in favor and all 49 Republicans opposed.
The bill was placed on the Senate legislative calendar but was never called up for debate or a final vote, and it died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The 49 Republican senators who blocked debate, plus the large donors, super PACs, dark-money groups, and incumbent lawmakers whose district lines, disclosure exemptions, and ethics rules the bill would have changed — all of them are better off because the bill never became law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The 49 Republican senators and big-money spenders

for.name: Jeff Merkley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled 48 cosponsors across the entire Senate Democratic conference.

for.name: Chuck Schumer
for.what_they_did: Brought the bill to the floor under an agreement requiring 60 votes to open debate, forcing every senator to cast a recorded vote; voted yes.

for.name: Amy Klobuchar
for.role: Chair, Senate Rules and Administration Committee
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill and held committee hearings on it, though the committee never reported it favorably.

for.name: 48 Democratic and 2 independent senators
for.what_they_did: All 50 voted to discharge the committee and open floor debate; none opposed.

against.name: 49 Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: All 49 voted against the motion to open debate, keeping the bill off the floor.

against.name: Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Voted against opening debate and led the Senate Republican opposition to the bill.

sides.party_line_note: The vote split perfectly by party: all 48 Democrats and 2 independents voted to open debate, and all 49 Republicans voted no, 50-49 against the 60 needed.
